title: Friday After Next
full_review:
Three times is definitely not the charm when it comes to "Friday After Next," New Line's sequel to the Ice Cube vehicles -- 1995's "Friday" and 2000's "Next Friday."

As haphazardly directed by Marcus Raboy, and again written and produced by Ice Cube, the indulgent depiction of recreational drug use is not funny given the reality of how many lives have been disastrously affected by substance abuse. Nor are the racial epithets and the stereotyping of African-Americans an enjoyable element of this crude comedy.

The film takes place in Los Angeles on Christmas Eve, as cousins and roommates Craig (Ice Cube) and Day-Day (Mike Epps) awake to find a masked Santa absconding with their presents and the rent money. The clueless cousins head off to their new jobs as strip-mall security guards but are more interested in smoking joints in the alley, and their older-but-no-wiser uncle (Don "D.C." Curry) joins right in. The cops who checked out the robbery complaint are also seen smoking dope in their police car.

Meanwhile back at home the pair's landlady (BeBe Drake) breaks into their apartment and steals some of their weed for herself while her pumped-up ex-con son (Terry Crews) looks forward to assaulting the twosome if they don't fork over the rent money.

The foul-mouthed cousins get fired by the end of the day and throw a party where the ex-con attempts to attack a puny pimp (Katt Williams) but finds himself on the receiving end of an extended scene of genital torture. The stream of toilet humor, punctuated by the ever-present four-letter words, is another abrasive element of the picture.

It all adds up to a pretty miserable excuse for a movie in which, according to the press notes, "Craig and Day-Day learn about the true meaning of the holiday season." They must have edited that scene out.

Due to a positive depiction of recreational drug use, constant rough language, intermittent profanity, some violence, sexual situations with gross references, frequent racial epithets, stereotyping and toilet humor, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
